extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of theology and biblical exegesis (clergy, learned readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining the proper signification of key biblical terms (e.g., body, spirit, angel, inspiration, kingdom of God) when interpreting Scripture, using scriptural usage and contextual cues rather than vulgar or modern assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine constant signification of scriptural words
rubrics_metrics.description: The foundation of sound reasoning is to settle the constant signification of words in Scripture; meanings should be derived from how words are used in Scripture, not from the writer's private will or common vulgar use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before inferring doctrinal conclusions, identify the sense a word carries across Scriptural contexts. Where ambiguity persists, prefer meanings evident in Scripture itself; if none fit, accept that the passage may be beyond human understanding and require submission of faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body (substance) — primary sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Body (or substance) in its most general sense denotes that which occupies space or a real part of the universe — things with dimension that can be divided and moved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'body' and 'substance' as synonymous when the text attributes extension, change, motion, or sensible qualities. Beware of self-contradictory locutions such as 'incorporeal substance.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Common-speech sense of body vs. spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: In common language, 'body' often denotes only those parts of the universe perceptible by touch or sight; 'spirit' often denotes subtle, airy substances (wind/breath) or phantasms of the imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When popular descriptions (e.g., 'spirits' as winds or 'ghosts' as phantasms) align with the scriptural context, prefer these common-sense readings rather than imposing metaphysical categories absent from the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirit — as wind or breath (physical/meteorological sign)
rubrics_metrics.description: In passages like Gen. 1:2 and Gen. 8:1, 'Spirit of God' can mean a wind or breath — an aire or motion that God causes, not God himself as a moved corporeal thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the text describes motion, diminishing waters, or other meteorological action, interpret 'spirit' as wind/breath (an external sign of God's action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirit — as extraordinary gifts of understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases such as 'spirit of wisdom' (e.g., Joseph, Exod. 28:3, Exod. 31) denote extraordinary abilities or divinely-given understanding, not a separate ghostly entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When 'spirit' qualifies intellectual gifts or skills (craftsmanship, wisdom, counsel), read it as a metaphor for bestowed talent or grace rather than a metaphysical intrusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirit — as extraordinary affections or zeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages that say 'the Spirit of God came upon' a person (Judges, Saul, etc.) often mean extraordinary zeal, courage, or passion (e.g., to deliver Israel), not possession by a disembodied ghost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where action is described as sudden zeal or fury in response to events, understand 'spirit' as heightened affect or inspiration to act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirit — as prophetic gift via dreams and visions
rubrics_metrics.description: When prophets speak 'by the Spirit,' the knowledge of future events is often via supernatural dreams or visions rather than an inner incorporeal ghost speaking within them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prophetic account connects to dreams/visions, construe 'spirit' as the faculty or experience of revelation (a supernatural appearance), not literal infusion of divine substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirit — as life (breath of life)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions like 'breath of life' (Gen. 2:7) or 'spirit in my nostrils' mean simply that a person is alive; 'spirit' here denotes vital motion or life, not an immaterial occupant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate such idioms as references to life/vitality rather than metaphysical dualism; e.g., 'spirit entered and set me on my feet' = regained strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirit — as subordination to authority (office or commission)
rubrics_metrics.description: In contexts like Numbers 11 and Deut. 34:9, 'spirit' indicates authority or ordination conferred by a superior (e.g., Moses to Joshua), i.e., a delegated capacity to act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When 'spirit' is tied to appointment, leadership, or confession of doctrine (e.g., 'spirit of Christ' meaning submission to his teaching), read it as institutional or doctrinal conformity rather than an ontological presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spirit — as aerial or subtle corporeal bodies (apparitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some appearances called 'spirits' or 'angels' may be thin, subtile bodies — substantial and extended (e.g., disciples seeing Jesus on the sea, pillars of cloud/fire), not mere fantasies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple witnesses perceive the appearance and the text treats it as shared, consider a corporeal (though subtle) substance rather than a private phantasm; such apparitions can be formed by God to manifest his will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid interpreting 'spirit' as literal infusion of God's substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms like 'filled with the Holy Spirit' or 'I will pour out my spirit' are metaphors signifying gifts, graces, or prophetic experiences; they are not to be understood as God being effused as a bodily substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject literalistic conceptions of God as a transferable substance; interpret 'inspiration' and 'pouring out' as promises of prophetic dreams, gifts, or dispositions rather than physical transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspiration — metaphorical guidance of writers' minds
rubrics_metrics.description: Scriptural 'inspiration' (e.g., 2 Tim. 3:16) most properly means God inclining the minds of writers to produce useful teaching, reproof, correction, and instruction, not infusion of divine substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish prophecy by dream/vision (supernatural experience) from 'inspiration' as God's providential guidance of an author's intellect; the Pentecost wind is an external sign of inward graces, not a literal airborne deity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angel = messenger; interpret by function not assumed ontology
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'angel' generally signifies a messenger of God, i.e., anything that shows extraordinary manifestation of God's presence (voice, dream, vision, pillar of cloud/fire), not necessarily a permanent immaterial being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read 'angel' according to its use: sometimes an angel is a vision, a voice, or a natural sign. Only where the text gives clear indications of permanence, location, and judgment should one infer a lasting, substantial angelic being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess angelic permanence and materiality from textual indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages in the New Testament (judgement of angels, eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels, Paul saying we will judge angels) suggest permanence and materiality; weigh such verses when inferring angelic nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the text attributes ordination, punishment, judgment, location, or resurrection-like properties to angels, prefer an interpretation that grants them permanence and (at least) subtle corporeality; avoid a priori claims of immateriality when scripture implies otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kingdom of God — prefer literal, covenantal civl-sovereignty reading
rubrics_metrics.description: In most Scriptural places the 'Kingdom of God' signifies a proper kingdom constituted by covenant (e.g., God's covenant with Abraham, Sinai renewal) — a civil sovereignty over a peculiar people — rather than merely metaphorical eternal felicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret 'kingdom' in its ordinary political sense when the context refers to covenants, land (Canaan), priests, or national election. Allow that in the New Testament 'kingdom' is sometimes used metaphorically (dominion over sin or sanctification), but default to the literal civic sense unless contextual cues indicate otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace origin and legal character of the Kingdom of God in texts
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand the Kingdom as arising from God's covenant with Abraham and renewed at Sinai (Exod. 19), implying a people who consented to be God's peculiar possession and a sacerdotal-royal constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting passages about the Kingdom, check for references to covenant, priesthood, election, and civic institutions; these indicate the political/commonwealth dimension rather than purely spiritual/eschatological meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer context-driven interpretation over inherited popular images
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not uncritically adopt common images (e.g., painted angels with wings; 'ghost' translations) that misrepresent the scriptural meanings; let the function and scriptural usage determine sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When popular or artistic representations conflict with scriptural indicators (motion, location, collective witness, office), revise understanding in favor of textual evidence. Where scripture remains obscure, accept the limits of human reason and practice doctrinal submission.
